name: Light Ivory
lede: Light Ivory is a pale, warm beige standardized by the German RAL paint system in 1927 and later carried into the American ISCC-NBS color dictionary, grammatically a lighter version of Ivory rather than its own invention.

sections.title: A lighter Ivory
sections.body: Light Ivory is RAL 1015, one of the original RAL 840 colors fixed by Germany's RAL paint-naming body in 1927, and it also appears as block 89 in the ISCC-NBS color-name dictionary of 1955, filed there as a pale yellow [1]. Its name is built or [[wheat]]: a brightness word in front of an existing color name, [[ivory]], rather than a name coined on its own [1]. In Munsell notation it sits at 0.1Y 8.5/2.5, and the nearest named color in our library, Beige, is only 3.4 units away [1]. Close lookalikes include [[cream]] and [[antique-white]], both warmer, paler neutrals from the same family [1]. As with any RAL swatch, the hex value here is a screen approximation of a printed paint chip, not a measured pigment [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this beige in 1,830 of 23,781 paintings, 7.7 percent, more common than 92 percent of our named colors, as photographed [2]. It plays a highlight in just over half of its appearances and peaks, unusually, in paintings from the 1100s, 14 percent of the handful we have from that century [2]. Xugu paints it most devotedly, in 9 of his 16 catalogued works [2]. The earliest dated example is from the year 900, more than a thousand years before RAL fixed the name in 1927; that gap is a reminder that the match is a look-alike hue, not proof of the paint itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
